reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: The rarest porphyria, an autosomal recessive deficiency of ALA dehydratase (porphobilinogen synthase), the second enzyme of haem biosynthesis
Presents with acute neurovisceral attacks resembling acute intermittent porphyria, including abdominal pain, vomiting and motor neuropathy
It is a non-cutaneous acute porphyria, as the accumulating substance is the neurotoxic precursor rather than a photoreactive porphyrin
The distinctive biochemical hallmark is markedly raised urinary ALA with normal or only slightly raised porphobilinogen, unlike the other acute porphyrias where PBG also rises
Urinary coproporphyrin III is characteristically increased, reflecting non-enzymatic conversion of accumulated substrate
Because the enzyme is inhibited by lead and depleted in tyrosinaemia, these acquired states must be excluded before attributing disease to the inherited defect
Management of attacks follows the principles for acute porphyrias with trigger avoidance, glucose loading and intravenous haem
reference.pathophysiology: ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria arises from near-complete deficiency of ALA dehydratase, the second enzyme of the haem pathway, which condenses two molecules of aminolaevulinic acid to form porphobilinogen. The block causes accumulation of ALA, the neurotoxic precursor believed to underlie the neurovisceral manifestations, while porphobilinogen production is impaired so PBG is not elevated. Some accumulated substrate is diverted to coproporphyrin III. The same enzyme is exquisitely sensitive to inhibition by lead and is functionally depleted in hereditary tyrosinaemia type I through succinylacetone, both of which can reproduce an identical biochemical and clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Lead poisoning (plumboporphyria), which inhibits the same enzyme
Hereditary tyrosinaemia type I with succinylacetone inhibition of the enzyme
Acute intermittent porphyria and other acute porphyrias
Guillain-Barre syndrome for the acute neuropathy
Surgical acute abdomen during an attack
Other causes of raised urinary ALA
additionalInvestigations: Urinary ALA (markedly raised) with porphobilinogen (normal or only mildly raised)
Blood lead level and, in children, exclusion of tyrosinaemia (succinylacetone)
Molecular genetic testing of the ALAD gene for confirmation and family screening
Nerve conduction studies where motor neuropathy is present
redFlags: Progressive motor weakness or respiratory compromise during an attack
Failure to exclude treatable lead poisoning or tyrosinaemia
Seizures or severe autonomic instability during an attack
Severe presentation in infancy or childhood
reference.prognosis: The condition is extremely rare and variable; some patients have severe recurrent attacks from childhood while others are milder, and prognosis depends on prompt recognition, exclusion of acquired mimics and avoidance of precipitants.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude lead poisoning and tyrosinaemia, which mimic the biochemistry exactly
Assuming all acute porphyrias raise porphobilinogen and discounting the diagnosis when PBG is normal
Prescribing porphyrinogenic drugs that may precipitate attacks
Overlooking the recessive inheritance when counselling families
Delaying enzyme and genetic confirmation in an unusually rare disorder
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
